newsitem.title: USA: FAA once weighed way to prevent fuel tank blast.
newsitem.headline: FAA once weighed way to prevent fuel tank blast.

text.p: U.S. aviation officials said on Thursday that flushing volatile vapours from empty airline fuel tanks was considered in the 1970s, but dropped in favour of better ways to prevent accidental explosions.

Ignition of the vapours in the empty centre fuel tank is believed a possible cause of the explosion of Trans World Airlines flight 800 in the Atlantic off Long Island on July 17, killing all 230 people on board.
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials said the crash might have been prevented if ignition in the empty tank was the cause and if vapour flushing had been required.
Investigators do not know yet if such an explosion might have been caused by a bomb or a mechanical malfunction.

The New York Times said on Thursday that a method proposed by the FAA 24 years ago to flush vapours from empty tanks to prevent an explosion by accidental ignition might have prevented the crash of the Boeing 747.

FAA officials said research on flushing vapours had been conducted as one method to prevent explosions, but was never proposed as a requirement for planes because better ways were found to remove ignition sources from the empty tanks.
They included ignition-proof pumps and keeping electronics out of the tanks. In addition, they said, new fuels were far less volatile than fuels used two decades ago.
Asked if the FAA was taking a new look at vapours, they said if investigators found a fuel-tank explosion was the cause, a remedy into vapour ignition would certainly be sought.
The Times said the aviation industry lobbied against the proposal because of its cost.
Responding, the Air Transport Association, a grouping of major U.S. airlines, said the FAA rejected fuel tank flushing in the 1970s, and it had concurred in the decision.
It added it would be willing to take at new look at vapour flushing when the TWA investigation was completed.
